gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a price for a standalone recorder that records a 4K60 source at 4K60. The ClonerAlliance UHD Halo (CA-989UH) does, for $366.50 at the maker's US store today. Every other candidate either drops 4K60 to 1080p60 or records 4K at 30 fps at most.
standout_why: I compared against the pages ChatGPT cited: the RecDual Dongle page, the UHD Pro knowledge-base page, the UHD Pro product page, the AVerMedia ER330 datasheet and page, and the Hauppauge (streameez) store page. None of them names the UHD Halo or any model that records 4K60. Each one stops at 1080p60 or 4K30 and only passes 4K60 through. Our own page (dealectric.com/best-standalone-hdmi-recorder, opened 2026-11-08) says 'Every sub-$300 recorder caps recording at 4K30' and leaves the Halo out. One uncited result in the first chat was the Halo user manual (static.cloner-alliance.com ca-989uh_user_manual.pdf). It may state the 4K60 spec, but I couldn't open it because the file is over 10 MB, and it would carry no price. Rivals therefore have part of the spec at most, and none has the price or the comparison with the other models.
decides: If the source is a 4K60 console or player and the shopper wants 4K60 files, the UHD Halo at $366.50 is the only pick in this category. The next model up that records 2160p60 is Blackmagic's HyperDeck Shuttle 4K Pro at $1,695. Every cheaper model loses here: ZowieREC 4K ($199), UHD Pro ($278.50) and UHD Pro Max ($295.80) record 4K30 at best, and RecDual ($143.50), HD PVR Pro 60 ($129.90), EzRecorder 330G ($179.99, out of stock) and HyperDeck Shuttle HD ($575) record 1080p60 at most. If 1080p60 is enough, the cheapest in-stock option is the Hauppauge HD PVR Pro 60 at $129.90, which records to an SD card. The RecDual Dongle is next at $143.50.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: From storecheck.py search on store.cloner-alliance.com: price 366.5, no compare-at price, available true. A direct product call got HTTP 429. The maker's product page also shows $366.50.

findings.label: Max recording
findings.value: 3840 x 2160 at 60 fps, H.264/H.265, up to 50 Mbps, with 4K60 passthrough
findings.note: Spec table lists max recording resolution '3840 x 2160 @ 60fps' and bitrate '8/16/24/32/50 Mbps'. Storage is USB 3.0 Type-A and TF card. The page says 'Any HDCP protected sources are NOT supported' and that it 'does not support HDR content'. The maker also calls it 'the only true 4K60 capture box on the market', which is the maker's own claim and not tested.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Where it loses: the store text says 'up to 4K@60fps HDMI passthrough and up to 4K@30fps standalone recording', so a 4K60 source can't be recorded at 4K60.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Where it loses: 'Up to 4K@30fps recording' with 4K60 passthrough. It costs $70.70 less than the Halo ($366.50 - $295.80) and records half the frame rate at 4K.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Where it loses: records 'up to 1080p@60fps' with 4K60 passthrough, and only to a 'TF (microSD) card', with no USB drive. ChatGPT showed this card at $143.50, which matches.

findings.label: Price, maker US store

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Where it loses: records 1080p60 with only 4K30 input support, at nearly UHD Pro money. Its distinguishing features are a 3-inch LCD and a battery rated for up to 2.5 hours.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Where it loses: records 1080p60 only, with 4K30 input, and costs $318.90 for a 7-inch LCD and analog inputs. The Halo, which records 4K60, is $47.60 more.

findings.source_title: HD PVR Pro 60 – Hauppauge Webstore for North America
findings.note: SKU 1684, no strikethrough price. This is the cheapest standalone recorder priced today.

findings.label: Standalone recording spec
findings.value: HDMI in up to 4K60, records 1080p60 H.264 to SD card (tested up to 512 GB); standalone mode needs a 5 V, 0.9 A or greater USB power supply
findings.note: The page says FAT32 'will segment a recording every 4Gb' and recommends exFAT. Where it loses: 1080p60 ceiling, SD card only, and no HDCP statement on the page. The US Hauppauge page failed a TLS certificate check.

findings.label: Price, maker US page
findings.note: Where it loses: HDMI input only, records 1080p/1080i (H.264, ProRes, DNxHD), and has no 4K input. ChatGPT showed '$295.00 · B&H Photo' for this model, which is $280 below the maker's price. I couldn't verify that price (B&H returned 403).

findings.label: Price and recording cap, maker US page
findings.value: $1,695; Ultra HD up to 2160p60 (H.265, ProRes, DNx), 12G-SDI + HDMI
findings.note: This is the next standalone 4K60 recorder above the Halo. $1,695 - $366.50 = $1,328.50 more.

unsourced: The B&H price for the HyperDeck Shuttle HD that ChatGPT showed ($295). bhphotovideo.com returned 403, so only the maker's $575 is sourced.
The Zowietek ZowieREC 4K price after the automatic checkout discount ('up to 13% off' until 2026-11-15) and separate prices for the two variants. The store page shows only $199.
A US store price for the original AVerMedia EzRecorder 330 (ER330). The maker page has only a Where to Buy link, and the US store lists just the 330G.
The maximum storage capacity for the UHD Halo. The product page lists USB 3.0 and TF card with FAT32/exFAT/NTFS but no capacity, and the manual PDF (ca-989uh_user_manual.pdf) was too large to open.
Any independent reviewer's test confirming that the UHD Halo actually records 4K60. I found none within the call budget, so the 4K60 claim rests on the maker's spec table.
An HDCP statement for the Hauppauge HD PVR Pro 60 and the Zowietek ZowieREC 4K. Neither maker page I opened mentions HDCP.
